title: Stoic in success
hookLine: the horse is handsome, not you

cards: The promotion comes through. Or the grade, or the offer on the house, or the post that suddenly has ten thousand likes. For a day or two, you walk differently.
You catch yourself rereading the congratulations. You're a little more confident in meetings, a little less patient with people who haven't had your luck. Nobody warns you about this part.
There's plenty of advice about failure, and almost none about winning. The Stoics thought success was a test too, sometimes a harder one.

teach.h: PROUD OF THE HORSE, NOT YOURSELF.

teach.b: Epictetus, in the Handbook: don't take pride in any excellence that isn't yours. If a horse were proud and said, I'm handsome, that could be borne.
But when you say, I have a handsome horse, you're proud of the horse's good, not your own. In success, a lot of what we're proud of is horse: the title, the money, the numbers, the luck of timing.

What's yours is the effort, the honesty, how you treated people on the way. Second, a warning Marcus wrote to himself. In book six he tells himself: take care not to be Caesarified, not to be dyed in that color.
He was the most powerful man in the Roman world, and he could feel the purple seeping in.
The Greek is a single word he seems to have coined, apokaisarōthēs, almost funny, as if becoming Caesar were a disease you could catch. Third, how to hold a win.
In book eight Marcus describes a way of having good things: receive them without arrogance, and let them go easily.

He'd watched his adoptive father, Antoninus Pius, use the comforts of power without showing off and without fussy refusals, enjoying them when present and not missing them when gone. Fourth, why it matters.
Success changes how we see other people. It's easy to think the win proves we're better.

teach.h: THE SAME PERSON, A DIFFERENT HORSE.
teach.b: The Stoics would say: you're the same person you were last week, with a different horse.
Enjoy the horse. Thank the people who helped. Stay kind to those still waiting for theirs.

how: Some Stoic practitioners meet a success by separating what was luck or help from their own effort, thanking those who helped, and watching for arrogance.

o: a Stoic teacher who refused every comfort of power
the emperor Marcus warned himself never to become
the adoptive father who enjoyed power's comforts lightly

games.q: not my horse — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus warned himself not to be Caesarified
Meditations 6.30: don't be dyed in that color.
the Stoics thought success needed no care, only failure did
they saw success as a test too, a risk of arrogance.
Epictetus says being proud of a fine horse is pride in your own good
it's pride in the horse's good, not yours.

games.q: you're Marcus, the most powerful man in the Roman world. what do you write in your private notebook?
o: take care not to be Caesarified
games.why: Meditations 6.30: don't be turned into a Caesar, dyed in the purple; stay simple, good, kind.

practice: Think of one recent win, small or large, and let yourself feel glad; that's allowed. Then sort it gently: what part was the horse, luck, timing, other people's help, and what part was yours, effort, honesty, care?
Hold both, and picture one person who helped make it happen.

wordCard.voice: Antoninus Pius, whom Marcus watched use the comforts of power without showing off and without missing them when they were gone. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Meditations 6.30: don't be Caesarified, a word Marcus seems to have coined.

carryVoice: Your line: not my horse. Glad of the win, and clear about what was yours. Until tomorrow.
